section.title: The Bride's Invitation
section.sectionRationale: The bridegroom praises his bride once more, now from feet to head, delighting in her whole person, and declares how fair and pleasant she is. The bride answers with the second great refrain of belonging, I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me, and then invites him away to the countryside and the vineyards, where she will give him her love. Desire here is mutual, glad, and freely offered within covenant.
section.thesis: The bridegroom's delight in his bride is met by her glad, confident answer: she belongs to him and his desire is for her, and she invites him out to the vineyards to give him her love, mutual desire offered freely within covenant.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the bridegroom's praise from feet to head, captivated by his bride; her answering refrain, I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me; and her springtime invitation to the vineyards, there I will give you my love.

verses.text: How beautiful are your sandaled feet, O daughter of the prince! The curves of your thighs are like jewels, the handiwork of a master.
Your navel is a rounded goblet; it never lacks blended wine. Your waist is a mound of wheat encircled by the lilies.
Your breasts are like two fawns, twins of a gazelle.
Your neck is like a tower made of ivory; your eyes are like the pools of Heshbon by the gate of Bath-rabbim; your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, facing toward Damascus.
Your head crowns you like Mount Carmel, the hair of your head like purple threads; the king is captured in your tresses.
How fair and pleasant you are, O {{ahavah|love}}, with your delights!
Your stature is like a palm tree; your breasts are clusters of fruit.
I said, “I will climb the palm tree; I will take hold of its fruit.” May your breasts be like clusters of the vine, the fragrance of your breath like apples,
and your mouth like the finest wine. May it flow smoothly to my beloved, gliding gently over lips and teeth.
I belong to my {{dodi|beloved}}, and his {{teshuqah|desire}} is for me.

units.label: Come to the vineyards
units.note: there I will give you my love

verses.text: Come, my beloved, let us go to the countryside; let us spend the night among the wildflowers.
Let us go early to the vineyards to see if the vine has budded, if the blossom has opened, if the pomegranates are in bloom, there I will give you my love.
The mandrakes send forth a fragrance, and at our door is every delicacy, new as well as old, that I have treasured up for you, my beloved.

ahavah.gloss: Love. The bridegroom calls the bride herself O love, with your delights; the same word that crowns the Song at 8:6, covenant love here personified in the beloved and delighted in.

dodi.gloss: My beloved. The bride's recurring name for the man; her refrain, I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me, is the settled language of mutual, covenant belonging.

teshuqah.gloss: Desire, longing. A rare word: it appears of the woman's desire toward her husband in Genesis 3:16 and of sin crouching in Genesis 4:7. Here it is turned to joy, his desire is for me, longing redeemed and freely returned within covenant love.

basic.context: The bridegroom praises his bride once more, this time from her feet upward, delighting in her whole person and crying, how fair and pleasant you are, O love. He longs to draw near to her. The bride answers with the second great refrain of the Song, I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me, and then she takes the lead, inviting him out to the countryside and the vineyards in the fresh of the morning, there I will give you my love. Desire here is mutual, unhurried, and freely offered.
basic.hermeneutics: On the plain level this is the glad, mutual desire of husband and wife, freely given within their covenant, the wife now inviting as gladly as the husband praises. The imagery is poetic and evocative, not clinical. The word desire is striking: it is the very word used in Genesis 3 for the strained longing between the sexes, here healed and turned to joy. Within the whole Bible, the mutual belonging and the longing satisfied point to the love between Christ and His church.
basic.originalLanguages: The bridegroom calls the bride herself ahavah, love, and says his heart is captured. She answers with dodi, my beloved, and the rare word teshuqah, desire, the very word from Genesis 3:16, now redeemed: his desire is for me. Then she invites him to the vineyards, there I will give you my love, longing freely returned rather than grasped.
basic.typology: The mutual desire of bridegroom and bride, each glad to belong to the other, foreshadows the love between Christ and His church, His delight in her and her longing for Him. The word desire, once strained by the fall, healed here into joy, points to the restoration of love in Christ.
basic.christ: The refrain his desire is for me pictures the astonishing truth that Christ desires His people, that He set His love on the church and longs for her. And the bride's glad invitation pictures the church's answering longing, come, my beloved, the same cry the Spirit and the bride raise at the close of Scripture, come, Lord Jesus.
basic.god: God is not reluctant toward His people; His desire is for them. He heals what the fall strained, turning grasping and rule into mutual delight, and He receives the love His people freely offer. The intimacy of husband and wife is His good gift, and He is not embarrassed by joy.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 3:16, the word desire, strained by the fall and healed here. Ephesians 5:31 to 32, the one flesh mystery of Christ and the church. Revelation 22:17, the Spirit and the bride say, come. Isaiah 62:5, as a bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so will your God rejoice over you.
basic.oneStory: Praise is met with glad answer: the bride belongs to her beloved, his desire is for her, and she freely invites him to the vineyards. Mutual longing, once strained by the fall, is healed into joy, a picture of the love between Christ and His church, who together say, come.

context.literary:
Song 7:1-13 is the fifth and longest of the Song's descriptive poems, and it breaks the pattern of the earlier ones in two ways. Chapters 4 and 6 describe the bride from the head downward; this one begins at the sandaled feet and climbs, so that the poem arrives at her crown, hair and then her whole stature. The man has stopped admiring a figure at a distance and is drawing near. The poem keeps its own direction: in verse 8 he says 'I will climb the palm tree,' and the ascent of the description becomes the ascent of desire.

The poem also changes grammatical mood. Verses 1 to 5 are statements, 'your neck is like a tower.' Verses 6 to 9 turn into direct exclamation and then into wish: 'I said, I will climb,' and 'May your breasts be like clusters.' Verse 9 slides without a break into the bride's voice, finishing the man's thought, and verse 10 is hers. The whole speech is a conversation, with the two voices finishing each other's lines.

Verse 10 is the hinge. The Song states possession three times, and the sequence moves: 'My beloved is mine and I am his,' Song 2:16; 'I belong to my beloved and he belongs to me,' 6:3; and now 'I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me.' The first two are balanced and almost symmetrical. The third drops the second half and puts something new in its place, desire directed at her. After that the bride does the leading: four invitations in verses 11 and 12, all of them 'Come' or 'Let us,' and the closing promise 'there I will give you my love.'

The geography of the praise is worth noticing. The man likens his bride to pools at Heshbon, a tower of Lebanon facing Damascus, and Mount Carmel. These are the high and distant places of the land, and his love sees the whole country in her.
context.historical:
The places named in verses 4 and 5 are real and well known to a first hearer. Heshbon was the city of Sihon the Amorite, taken by Israel, Numbers 21:25-26, and lay east of the Jordan. Lebanon was the cedar country to the north, and Damascus the great city beyond it. Carmel is the wooded headland on the Mediterranean, the mountain of Elijah's contest, 1 Kings 18:19. The picture is of an entire world gathered into one body.

The poem calls her 'daughter of the prince.' In a world of arranged marriage and court alliances, such a phrase was a mark of honour, though the Hebrew word translated 'prince' can also mean someone noble or generous in spirit, and the poet may be playing on both. The sandals add to the picture of dignity.

The agricultural world supplies the rest of the images: wheat in heaps, wine that never runs out, palm trees with their clusters of dates, and the vine in bud. The setting of the invitation is the early spring vineyard, the same season as Song 2:10-13, when the winter is past. Mandrakes in verse 13 were evidently prized as an aid to love and fertility, which fits Rachel and Leah's bargaining over them, Genesis 30:14-16. Placing them 'at our door' turns the rumour of an old remedy into a picture of a house prepared. The footnote for verse 11 notes that the word translated 'wildflowers' might instead be 'henna blossoms or villages'; either way the lovers are leaving the town for the open country.
context.canonical:
This passage has three particularly rich lines of connection. The first is with Genesis. The bride's word 'desire,' teshuqah, in 7:10 is found in only two other places in the Hebrew Bible: Genesis 3:16, where it is part of the sentence on the woman, and Genesis 4:7, where sin's desire is for Cain. In the first two cases the word marks something strained or dangerous. In the Song it is placed in the mouth of a woman who rejoices that the desire is for her.

The second line is with the rest of the wisdom literature. Proverbs 5:18-19 tells a husband to rejoice in the wife of his youth and to be 'captivated by her love forever.' The same book warns against the counterfeit, where an adulteress invites a man with similar words, Proverbs 7:18. The Song's glad invitation is the honest version of what the adulteress imitates.

The third is the New Testament's teaching on marriage. Paul says that husband and wife do not hold authority over their own bodies but each over the other's, 1 Corinthians 7:3-5, which is the language of mutual belonging in verse 10. Hebrews 13:4 says marriage is honoured by all and its bed undefiled. And Ephesians 5:31-32 names the 'profound mystery' that the one-flesh union speaks of Christ and the church. The vineyard setting also joins the prophets' use of the vineyard as the place where the LORD looks for fruit, Isaiah 5:1-2.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The poet means to show that desire inside marriage is good, mutual and unashamed. He does so in language that a modern reader may find startlingly frank, and he does not apologise for it. The reader is meant to hear that bodily love is not a regrettable concession but a gift, and that the God who made the body made delight with it.

He also means to teach by shape. The man's praise rises from the feet and ends in the vow to climb the palm tree, and the woman's reply takes over the poem and gives it its direction. The first hearers would have noticed that she is not passive. She states her belonging, she names the place and the time, and she promises to give her love. The poem does not teach that a wife is an object of praise. It teaches that she and her husband are partners in desire.

The central line is verse 10, which for the author is the answer to an older sorrow. Those who knew Genesis 3:16 would have heard in 'his desire is for me' a lifting of the shadow. The poet means to say that in covenant love the old distortion does not have the last word.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The poem records one couple's praise and invitation. It does not instruct anyone on how to speak to a spouse, nor is the series of bodily similes a script. A husband who tried to repeat them would sound absurd, since the images belong to another culture's picture of beauty. What is prescribed is not the vocabulary but the posture: delight, belonging, and freedom from shame.

The passage describes a marriage in which the wife takes the initiative, and it does not rebuke her. That matches Paul's balance in 1 Corinthians 7:3-5, where each owes the other, and neither one rules.

Two cautions apply. The poem is addressed within covenant, and Hebrews 13:4 says that the marriage bed is to be kept undefiled; the Song gives no ground for treating its language as a charter for desire outside marriage. And the language of Genesis 3:16 is a description of a world under judgment, not a commandment, so the Song's reversal should not be read as proof that all marriages will be free of strain. It is a sign and a promise, and believers pursue it by grace.

debates.question: Does 'his desire is for me' deliberately reverse Genesis 3:16?

views.label: Yes, a deliberate reversal
views.case: The word teshuqah appears in only three places, Genesis 3:16, Genesis 4:7 and Song 7:10, and in the Genesis texts it describes a distorted or dangerous longing. The Song places the same word in a setting where the desire flows towards the woman and is glad. On this view the poet has Eden in mind throughout, and the sentence on the woman is being lifted in the covenant love of the lovers.

views.label: A shared word with a different sense
views.case: Others point out that the word simply means longing or craving, and that the context decides. In Genesis 3:16 the context is judgment, in Genesis 4:7 it is sin, and in the Song it is love. There is no need to suppose that the poet had the earlier verses in mind, and the likenesses between the verses may be accidental.

views.label: A reversal in the canon even if not in the poet's mind
views.case: A third approach grants that the first hearers may not have thought of Genesis, but says that the Bible as a whole reads one passage in light of another. A reader who has Genesis 3:16 in view hears the Song as a sign of what grace restores, whether or not the human author intended that.

debates.bearing: The rarity of the word makes the first view attractive, and it fits the Song's many echoes of Eden. But the passage does not depend on it. Even without the link to Genesis, verse 10 teaches mutual belonging, and the link makes it richer.

debates.question: How should the frank imagery of verses 1 to 9 be read?

views.label: Plainly, as the poetry of married love
views.case: The images describe a husband's delight in his wife's body, and the Bible treats such delight as good within marriage, Proverbs 5:18-19. The text does not blush, and neither need the reader.

views.label: Allegorically, as a code for the church
views.case: Much of the church's early and medieval tradition read each image as a spiritual reality: the feet as the preachers, the neck as the church's teaching, and so on. Many interpreters since have judged that this goes beyond the text, since the poem itself gives no key.

views.label: Plainly first, then as a picture of Christ and the church
views.case: The central path is to take the poem at face value and then to follow the New Testament's own warrant, Ephesians 5:31-32, in seeing that human marriage is a sign of a greater union. The lesson is drawn from the relationship, not from individual body parts.

debates.bearing: The third path guards against both embarrassment and fantasy. It lets the text mean what it says and links it to Christ at the level where the New Testament itself makes the link.

study.originalLanguages:
The word 'desire' in verse 10 is teshuqah, from a root that carries the sense of longing or craving. It is one of the most carefully watched words in the Song. It occurs three times in the whole Hebrew Bible. In Genesis 3:16 the woman's desire is 'for your husband,' and in Genesis 4:7 sin's desire is for Cain, so that the word names a pull towards something that may rule. In Song 7:10 it is the man's desire, and it is for her. The movement from the woman's desire for the man to the man's desire for the woman is part of what makes the verse feel like a healing.

The verb of belonging is a simple one. The Hebrew says, literally, 'I to my beloved and he upon me his desire.' There is no verb of possession in the line, and the BSB supplies 'belong.' This is the third form of the Song's refrain, and the change is in the second half: where 2:16 and 6:3 said that the beloved is hers and she is his, the last version says that his desire is directed at her. The three statements move from possession to desire.

The word dodi, 'my beloved,' comes from the Hebrew word dod, which means love, especially the physical expression of love. The plural dodim is found in Proverbs 7:18, 'Let us delight in loving caresses,' and in Ezekiel 16:8, where the LORD sees that Jerusalem 'was old enough for love.' The Song's favourite name for the man is therefore 'my lover.' The same family gives the word for mandrakes in verse 13, dudaim, a plant known for its supposed power to arouse love, Genesis 30:14. The poet may be playing on the sound: 'the mandrakes give fragrance,' and 'I will give you my dodai,' my love, in the same breath.

In verse 6 the bride is called 'love,' ahavah, and her 'delights,' taanugim, are the plural of a word built on the same root as oneg, the 'delight' that Isaiah 58:13 says the Sabbath should be. The word refers to pleasure and luxury in the best sense, and the bride is the embodiment of such pleasure.

The invitation 'Let us go early' uses a verb that means to rise at the start of the day, and the effect is of an eager, unhurried morning. And in verse 13 the bride says she has 'treasured up' delicacies for her beloved. The verb tsafan is the one the psalmist uses of hiding God's word in his heart, Psalm 119:11, and it means to store something carefully against a future need. What she has prepared is not an improvisation. It is a stored gift, kept for him alone.

One more feature of the Hebrew should be noted. The bride's speech is full of 'give.' Verse 12 says, 'there I will give you my love,' using the common verb natan, to give. The verse makes love a gift rather than a possession, which links back to the Song's close, where love 'cannot be bought,' Song 8:7.

typology.type: I belong to my beloved, Song 7:10
typology.fulfillment: The refrain of belonging is taken up in the New Testament as the believer's identity. Paul says 'You are not your own; you were bought at a price,' 1 Corinthians 6:19-20, and writes that believers died to the law 'that you might belong to another, to Him who was raised from the dead,' Romans 7:4. Jesus says of His sheep that no one can snatch them from His hand, John 10:27-28. The escalation is that the belonging rests on His purchase. The type falls short because in marriage belonging is mutual and equal, while the church's belonging to Christ is that of the creature to the Lord.

typology.type: His desire is for me: the curse of Genesis 3:16 lifted
typology.fulfillment: The pull between man and woman that Genesis 3:16 describes as strained is shown here as glad. The New Testament says Christ redeemed us from the curse by becoming a curse for us, Galatians 3:13, and that in Christ the relationship of husband and wife is taught by His self-giving love, Ephesians 5:25. The healing is therefore real in Christ, and it is begun now in marriages and in the church. The type falls short because the Song cannot remove the curse; the full removal comes only when there is no longer any curse, Revelation 22:3.

typology.type: The bride who invites and gives: 'Come' in the vineyard, Song 7:11-13
typology.fulfillment: The bride's invitation to go to the vineyard and her promise to give her love correspond to the Spirit and the bride saying 'Come,' Revelation 22:17, and to the church's answer to the Lord who says He is coming soon, Revelation 22:20. They also answer the Lord's own invitation to the wilderness and the vineyards given back, Hosea 2:14-15. The type falls short because the Song's longing is satisfied in a day in the vineyard, while the church's longing waits for Christ's coming.

typology.type: Treasure laid up, new and old, Song 7:13
typology.fulfillment: The bride has stored 'every delicacy, new as well as old' at the door. Jesus uses nearly the same words of the scribe trained for the kingdom, who 'brings out of his storeroom new treasures as well as old,' Matthew 13:52. The correspondence is a verbal echo and not a claim that the Song was written with that verse in mind, so the link should be held lightly. It suggests that what the church has stored in the old covenant and the new is laid out for the Lord who comes.

study.christ:
The passage does not mention Christ, and the first reading should remain a husband's delight in his wife. But the line from the poem to Christ is drawn by the New Testament itself in Ephesians 5:31-32, and it runs through three themes.

The first is belonging. 'I belong to my beloved' is what every believer says to Christ. The belonging is bought: 'You are not your own; you were bought at a price,' 1 Corinthians 6:20. Yet it is not the belonging of a captive. Jesus says of His sheep, 'I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one can snatch them out of My hand,' John 10:28. The refrain of the Song gives an affectionate, personal voice to what the New Testament states in doctrine.

The second is the surprise of verse 10, 'his desire is for me.' In the Song this means a man wants his wife. In the gospel it means something far more astonishing, that the Lord wants His people. Jesus says before the cross, 'I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before My suffering,' Luke 22:15. The Son did not come grudgingly. The writer of Hebrews says that He endured the cross for the joy set before Him, Hebrews 12:2. The word desire, which Genesis uses of a fractured longing, here names the Lord's desire for those He has chosen. And Galatians 3:13 tells how the curse of Genesis was carried: Christ redeemed us 'by becoming a curse for us.'

The third is the bride's invitation. 'Come, my beloved, let us go' becomes, at the end of Scripture, the Spirit and the bride saying 'Come!' Revelation 22:17. The church's longing for Christ is not a duty but a response, as John says, 'We love because He first loved us,' 1 John 4:19. In the Song the order is clear: first he says her beauty and his desire, and only then does she invite. The church loves Him in answer to His love.

There is also the matter of fruit. The vineyard is where the vines bud, the blossoms open and the pomegranates bloom, and the bride goes there to give her love. Hosea promises that Israel will 'blossom like the lily' and that those who dwell in His shade 'will grow grain and blossom like the vine,' Hosea 14:5-7. The fruitfulness of the church is the fruit of her union with her Lord, which is Paul's point in Romans 7:4: we belong to Him 'in order that we might bear fruit to God.'

A caution is needed. The anatomical images of the first nine verses do not each stand for a doctrine. The honest link to Christ is the relationship as a whole: a bridegroom who desires, a bride who belongs, and a love given and received. To press each image into a symbol of the church is to go beyond what the text supplies.
study.god:
The first thing this passage shows about God is that He is the giver of delight. The poem is unembarrassed, and that matters for the doctrine of creation. The God who said that everything He made was very good, and who brought the woman to the man, made bodies and made desire. Proverbs 5:18-19 and Hebrews 13:4 hold both parts of what a believer must say: marriage is honoured, and its joy is to be received and guarded. Any picture of God that makes Him hostile to pleasure is contradicted by this book being in Scripture at all.

The second is that God is a God of belonging. The refrain that the bride speaks says that she is not alone, not self-owned and not adrift. Scripture says the same of those who trust Him: 'I will be their God, and they will be My people.' The covenant formula in its various places repeats this belonging, and Jesus' word that no one can snatch His sheep out of His hand, John 10:28, gives it firmness. God does not treat His own as a changing set of acquaintances.

The third is that God restores what has been distorted. Genesis 3:16 records the sentence in which the desire between man and woman is twisted into contest. Here the same word appears in a setting where it is gift, and the God who judged is also the God who heals. This is how God works throughout the Bible: He does not abandon the fallen creation but begins, within it, to make things new. A marriage where each delights to serve the other is evidence that He is doing so.

The fourth is that God desires His people. The text is about human lovers, but the prophets use the same shape for the LORD's love for Israel. Isaiah 62:5 says that as a bridegroom rejoices over a bride, so will your God rejoice over you. The Lord of Hosts is not driven by need, since He lacks nothing, and so His desire is freely given. The apostle John says that love begins with Him, 1 John 4:19.

The fifth is that God invites. The bride makes the invitation to the vineyards, and in doing so she shows a picture of the God who says, 'Come, all you who are thirsty,' Isaiah 55:1, and who in the last page of Scripture says, 'let the one who desires the water of life drink freely,' Revelation 22:17. The offer of grace is genuine and open.

For worship, the passage teaches that gladness is a fitting response to God. Our praise should not be grudging or merely dutiful. It should resemble the speech of the beloved who says 'I belong to my beloved,' with confidence, joy and without shame, since His desire for us was first.

crossReferences.note: The first of the three places where the word desire occurs. The woman's longing for her husband is placed under the sentence of judgment, and the next clause says he will rule. Set beside Song 7:10, it shows how the poem takes a word that began in sorrow and gives it back to joy.

The second occurrence. Sin crouches at Cain's door and desires him, but he must master it. This verse shows the word's dark potential, and sets the Song's use of it in sharper relief: the same pull, but in love it is welcomed.

The man's spring invitation, when the winter is past and the vines spread their fragrance. In 7:11-13 the bride answers with an invitation of her own to the same season, so that the Song's two voices now call each other out to the vineyards.
The middle form of the refrain: 'I belong to my beloved and he belongs to me.' Reading it just before 7:10 shows the progress, from mutual possession to the added thought that his desire is for her.

The father tells his son to rejoice in the wife of his youth and be captivated by her love. It is the wisdom teacher's version of what the Song sings, and it shows that the Song's frankness stands within the Bible's ordinary teaching on marriage.

Each spouse owes the other, and neither has authority over his or her own body but gives it to the other. This is the apostolic statement of mutual belonging and shows that the Song's 'I belong to my beloved' is not a poetic exaggeration but a pattern of married life.

Rachel and Leah bargain over mandrakes, the plant of the Song's verse 13, and the story shows how they were valued and what unhappy competition could surround them. The Song places them at the door as a free gift, a contrast with the bargaining of Genesis.

Paul quotes the one-flesh verse of Genesis 2:24 and calls it a profound mystery that speaks of Christ and the church. This is the apostolic warrant for reading the Song's marital love as a sign of the union between Christ and His people.

The LORD allures His people into the wilderness, speaks tenderly, gives back her vineyards, and is called 'my Husband.' The Song's bride takes her beloved to the vineyards to give him her love, and Hosea shows the greater love in which God does the same for His people.
The Spirit and the bride say 'Come!' The bride's invitation in the Song finds its final form here: the church's call to her Lord and to the thirsty, answering the love that was first given to her.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's first human conversation about love is Genesis 2:23 to 25, where a man receives a wife and the two stand together unashamed. Genesis 3 then records how the shame came, and Genesis 3:16 describes the first strain in that love: a desire that is no longer simple and a rule that is no longer gentle. Everything the Bible says afterward about marriage, from the unhappy households of the patriarchs to the prophets' pictures of a faithless wife, is told against that background. The Song of Solomon breaks the pattern for a moment. Here, in the middle of the fallen world, a husband and wife stand in a garden of their own and the old word 'desire' means joy.

Israel's story gives the picture its greater weight. The LORD takes Israel as His bride, Ezekiel 16:8, and the prophets call her back from her wandering, Hosea 2:14-16. The vineyard becomes the place where the relationship is tested, since He looks for fruit, Isaiah 5:1-2. In that long record the bridal imagery tells the people that God's claim on them is a claim of love. The Song's bride, who invites her husband to the vineyard and promises her love, shows what the faithful response would be.

The story comes to its centre in Christ, the bridegroom, who gave Himself so that the church might be presented glorious, Ephesians 5:25-27. In Him the broken desire is healed at its root, because He bore the curse, Galatians 3:13. The church's whole life is lived in the belonging that He bought, 1 Corinthians 6:20, and in the hope of His return. This is why the bride's 'Come' is not a mere flourish: it is the cry the church has made since the Ascension.

The story ends with a wedding. The marriage supper of the Lamb is announced, Revelation 19:7-9, and the last page has the Spirit and the bride saying 'Come!' while the Lord answers 'Yes, I am coming soon,' Revelation 22:17 and 22:20. In the new creation there will be no curse, and the strained desire of Genesis will be fully gone, replaced by a love that is only gift. The vineyard invitation of Song 7 is the small rehearsal of that day.

quiz.q: How does the bridegroom sum up his praise of the bride in 7:6?

options.text: How fair and pleasant you are, O love, with your delights.
options.note: He addresses the bride herself as love, delighting in her whole person.

options.text: How plain and forgettable you are.
options.note: He praises her as fair and pleasant, the opposite of forgettable.

options.text: How useful you are to me.
options.note: She is indeed precious to him, but his words are delight and affection in her whole person, not a matter of mere usefulness.

options.text: How much you must still improve.
options.note: He does lavish attention on her, but he delights in her as she is, calling her fair and pleasant, with nothing she must still improve.

quiz.q: What refrain does the bride speak in 7:10?

options.text: I belong to my beloved, and his desire is for me.
options.note: The second great refrain of belonging, now stressing his desire for her.

options.text: I hope my beloved might one day want me.
options.note: She does speak of belonging and his desire, but as a settled present reality, his desire is for me now, not merely a hope that he might one day want her.

options.text: My beloved desires many others.
options.note: His desire is for her alone, the language of exclusive covenant love.

options.text: I belong to myself alone.
options.note: She does have a real dignity of her own in the Song, but this refrain is mutual belonging, I am his and his desire is for me, not belonging to herself alone.

quiz.q: Why is the word desire in 7:10 so striking?

options.text: It is the word from Genesis 3:16 for strained longing after the fall, here healed into joy.
options.note: The same rare word, once a mark of the fall's strain, is turned to mutual delight.

options.text: It means the beloved is forced against his will.
options.note: It speaks of glad longing freely given, not compulsion.

options.text: It has no background elsewhere in Scripture.
options.note: It is indeed a rare and notable word, but it does have pointed echoes elsewhere, in Genesis 3 and 4, not no background at all.

options.text: It proves desire is always sinful.
options.note: It does carry the background of the fall from Genesis 3:16, but here that strained desire is healed into good, redeemed longing within covenant love, not proof that desire is always sinful.

quiz.q: What does the bride do after the refrain of belonging?

options.text: She invites her beloved out to the vineyards, there I will give you my love.
options.note: She takes the lead with a glad, free invitation.

options.text: She sends her beloved away.
options.note: She does call him to go out to the vineyards, but to go together, come my beloved, not to send him away.

options.text: She falls silent and withdraws.
options.note: She speaks up gladly and invites him.

options.text: She waits passively for him to act.
options.note: Her invitation does await his coming with her, but she is not passive; she takes the lead and initiates it.

quiz.q: How does his desire is for me point to the gospel?

options.text: It pictures Christ's glad longing for His church, who answers, come, my beloved.
options.note: Christ's love for His people is glad desire, and the church answers with longing, come, Lord Jesus.

options.text: It teaches that God only tolerates His people.
options.note: God does patiently bear with His people, but the refrain is desire and delight, far more than mere toleration.

options.text: It shows that God keeps His distance from His people.
options.note: The point is nearness and longing, his desire is for me.

options.text: It has nothing to do with Christ and the church.
options.note: It truly speaks of a human beloved's desire, yet the church has long heard here the mutual love of Christ and His people, Revelation 22:17, so it does point to the gospel.

questions: The bride hears, his desire is for me. Have you let yourself believe that Christ's love for you is glad longing and not cool duty, and how would that change today?
The word desire, strained by the fall, is healed here into joy. Where do you long to see God heal a strained or broken relationship into delight?
The bride takes the lead with a warm invitation, come, my beloved. Where might God be calling you to seek Him gladly rather than waiting passively?
She had treasured up delicacies, new and old, for her beloved. What have you stored up, in devotion or affection, to offer the Lord or those you love?
The Song presents mutual desire within covenant as good and joyful. How does that shape the way you think and speak about marriage, the body, and longing?

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew rendered mouth is literally palate; the versions differ on the last line, the Hebrew reading gliding gently over lips as we sleep.
Desire, teshuqah, is a rare word, used of the woman toward her husband in Genesis 3:16 and of sin in Genesis 4:7; here it is turned to joy, his desire is for me.
